newsitem.title: USA: Chrysler CEO sees lower March sales from year ago.
newsitem.headline: Chrysler CEO sees lower March sales from year ago.

text.p: Chrysler Corp. Chairman Robert Eaton said Wednesday the automaker's March U.S. light vehicle sales may dip slightly from a year ago, but argued that was not a sign the red-hot truck market was cooling off.
"Hell, no," Eaton adamently told reporters at the New York International Auto Show when asked if the truck market will slow down.

But in a bit of bad news for car enthusiasts, Chrysler officials revealed the spring 1997 introduction of the eagerly awaited new Prowler roadster has been pushed back because it is taking longer to perfect the all-aluminum body panels.

Eaton charged that Japanese automakers were flooding the U.S. market with imported vehicles and generous leasing incentives that were "forcing -- literally forcing -- the passenger car side of the market" up relative to the truck market.

While that makes the truck market look artificially weak, Eaton said the low fuel prices in the United States remain a key driver behind the boom in light trucks, and that was not likely to change any time soon.
"This is a function of fuel price and there is no political appetite in this country whatsoever to raise fuel taxes," he said.

March car sales at the U.S. No. 3 automaker are expected to fall slightly, while light trucks -- the segment that includes minivans, sport utility vehicles and pickup trucks -- will finish the month flat with March 1996, Eaton said.

He attributed the slowdown to a spring selling season that hasn't fully gotten into gear. Eaton said he did not believe the Federal Reserve Board's quarter point increase Tuesday in the federal funds rate -- the rate banks charge each other for overnight loans -- would hurt U.S. auto sales.

Overall, Eaton said he expected U.S. March total vehicle sales to finish at a seasonally adjusted annual sales rate of 15.2 million. Chrysler sold 136,642 light trucks and 81,231 cars for a total of 217,873 vehicles in March 1996.

Total sales of vehicles from Asian companies in the first two months of this year are up 13.8 percent, while their U.S. market share has climbed to 24.5 percent from 21.6 percent, according to the J.D. Power and Associates research firm. Unit sales from the Big Three U.S. automakers have fallen 4.3 percent, and market share has slipped to 71.8 percent from 75.2 percent, J.D. Power said.

Eaton's remarks came after Chrysler introduced its latest beefy light truck product, the Grand Cherokee 5.9 Limited. Billed as having the biggest engine available in a sport utility vehicle, the new Grand Cherokee comes with a 245-horsepower, 5.9-liter, V-8 engine that powers the vehicle from 0 to 60 mph in 7.3 seconds.

Chrysler also said it will bring back its "300" nameplate on a sports sedan next year based on its new-generation "LH" large car platform. The 300 nameplate was used on Chrysler's top-of-the-line cars in the 1950s and 1960s, which featured powerful engines combined with roominess and graceful styling.
Commenting on the Prowler, originally due out now, Chrysler officials said the pre-production process was taking longer than expected.
"There is not a problem with the Prowler," said Eaton, adding he will personally drive the car next week to determine if it is ready for volume production.
The car is a bold experiment for Chrysler with aluminum car construction and is being touted as the premier image car for the Plymouth brand.
"This car is so important for us that unless it's perfect, it's not going anywhere," said Martin Levine, general manager of the Chrysler, Plymouth and Jeep-Eagle brands.
Chrysler stock fell 62.5 cents to $30 in consolidated trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
